rows.stem: A compound undergoes complete tetramerization in a given organic solvent. The Van't Hoff factor 'i' is :
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is \(0{\cdot}25\).

That factor compares the number of particles ACTUALLY present with the number the formula predicts:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{observed number of particles}}{\text{expected number of particles}}\)

TETRAMERIZATION means four molecules combine into one, and COMPLETE tetramerization means every molecule does so. Four particles dissolved therefore become ONE:
\(i = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0{\cdot}25\)

The value being BELOW 1 is the signature of ASSOCIATION, and every colligative property falls in proportion — the depression in freezing point, the elevation in boiling point and the osmotic pressure are each a quarter of what the formula would predict.

A value ABOVE 1 would mean dissociation instead; \(4{\cdot}0\) is what complete dissociation into four ions would give, which is the reciprocal of this situation and the trap in the question.

rows.stem:
The half-life for a zero order reaction equals :
where R is the initial concentration.
rows.solution:
The half-life of a zero order reaction is \(\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\).

A zero order reaction proceeds at a CONSTANT rate, so the concentration falls linearly with time:
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)

At the half-life exactly half the reactant is left, so \([\mathrm{R}] = \frac{1}{2}[\mathrm{R}]_0\):
\(\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2} = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - k\,t_{1/2}\)

Rearranging gives \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\).

Two checks on the form of the answer. The half-life must be PROPORTIONAL to the starting concentration — at a fixed rate, twice as much takes twice as long — which rules out every option with the concentration in the denominator. And the units must come out as time: concentration divided by a zero order rate constant, which itself has the units of a rate.

Contrast FIRST order, where \(t_{1/2} = 0{\cdot}693/k\) and the starting concentration does not appear at all.

rows.stem: Which of the following structures represents \(\alpha\)-D-glucose ?

options.label: A
options.text: Structure (a) as printed — a drawn Haworth projection; see the attached figure.

options.label: B
options.text: Structure (b) as printed — a drawn Haworth projection; see the attached figure.

options.label: C
options.text: Structure (c) as printed — a drawn Haworth projection; see the attached figure.

options.label: D
options.text: Structure (d) as printed — a drawn Haworth projection; see the attached figure.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR OPTIONS are drawn Haworth pyranose projections of D-glucose, differing in the orientation of the anomeric —OH / —H at C-1 and in which ring carbon carries the —CH2OH group; (a) and (b) print CH2OH above the ring at the left-hand carbon while (c) and (d) print H there and place CH2OH on the right. The option block is a 2 x 2 array of ring drawings occupying the upper half of page idx 4 and MUST be attached as a crop.
rows.solution:
The first structure represents \(\alpha\)-D-glucose.

Two features identify it, and both must be right.

The \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) group must sit on the ring carbon at the far LEFT of the Haworth projection and point UPWARDS. That fixes the sugar as a D-glucopyranose. Only the first two structures satisfy this — in the third and fourth the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) is drawn on the RIGHT-hand ring carbon, where the anomeric centre belongs, so neither is a D-glucopyranose at all.

The hydroxyl on the ANOMERIC carbon — the right-hand carbon, next to the ring oxygen — must point DOWNWARDS, on the OPPOSITE side of the ring from the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). That is what \(\alpha\) means. The first structure has it down; the second has it UP, on the same side as the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\), which makes that one \(\beta\)-D-glucose.

So the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) forms differ at ONE centre only, and they interconvert in solution through the open chain form — which is why a fresh solution of either shows MUTAROTATION.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem: The ions of metals of Group 12 (Zn, Cd and Hg) have completely filled d orbitals and so they :

options.label: C
options.text: do not behave like transition metals

rows.solution:
They DO NOT BEHAVE LIKE TRANSITION METALS.

A transition element is defined as one with a PARTLY FILLED d subshell in the neutral atom or in one of its stable ions. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are \(d^{10}\) as atoms and \(d^{10}\) as their \(+2\) ions — filled in both — so the definition excludes them, and they are better described as d-BLOCK metals than as transition metals.

Every property that follows from a partly filled d subshell is therefore absent. Their compounds are WHITE, since there is no vacancy for a d-d electronic transition. They are DIAMAGNETIC, since no electron is unpaired. They show only ONE oxidation state in ordinary chemistry, \(+2\), and they are poor catalysts.

Their melting points are also unusually LOW rather than high, for the same underlying reason: with no unpaired d electrons available, only the two \(s\) electrons contribute to the metallic bond. Mercury is liquid at room temperature.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5NO_3]SO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]NO_3}\) exhibit :
rows.solution:
The pair exhibits IONIZATION ISOMERISM.

Ionization isomers have the same FORMULA but EXCHANGE an ion between the coordination sphere and the position of counter ion. Compare the two: in one the nitrate is the ligand and the sulphate the counter ion, and in the other they have swapped places.

They are easily told apart in solution, because each releases a DIFFERENT ion:
The one with sulphate outside gives a white precipitate with barium chloride, since free sulphate is present.
The one with nitrate outside gives no such precipitate, its sulphate being locked inside the coordination sphere; it responds instead to the tests for free nitrate.

Each fails the other's test, which is the practical meaning of the isomerism and the reason it is named for IONISATION.

Linkage isomerism would need an ambidentate ligand able to bind through either of two atoms, which is a different situation entirely.

rows.stem: Reaction of 1-phenyl-2-chloropropane with alcoholic KOH gives mainly :
rows.solution:
The main product is 1-PHENYLPROPENE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH{=}CH{-}CH_3}\).

Alcoholic potassium hydroxide supplies ALKOXIDE ions, which are strong bases and so cause ELIMINATION rather than substitution. The base removes a \(\beta\) hydrogen and the halide leaves, forming a double bond.

The substrate \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH(Cl){-}CH_3}\) offers a choice of \(\beta\) hydrogen — one from the benzylic \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) on one side, one from the methyl on the other — so two alkenes are possible.

Removing the BENZYLIC hydrogen wins, because the resulting double bond is CONJUGATED with the benzene ring. That conjugation extends the \(\pi\) system and stabilises the product, and it outweighs Saytzeff considerations here.

The other two options are alcohols, which would need AQUEOUS potassium hydroxide; in alcohol the reagent eliminates rather than substitutes.

rows.stem: When diethyl ether is heated with excess of HI, it produces :
rows.solution:
The product is ETHYL IODIDE — two molecules of it.

Cleaving an ether with hydroiodic acid begins by protonating the oxygen, after which iodide attacks one of the alkyl carbons:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)

With ONE equivalent the reaction stops there, giving an alkyl iodide and an alcohol. But the question specifies an EXCESS of hydroiodic acid, and the ethanol formed is itself attacked:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

So both halves end as ethyl iodide. Ethanol is the intermediate rather than the final product, which is the trap.

Methyl iodide could not form at all — there is no methyl group anywhere in diethyl ether.

rows.stem: The reduction of ethanenitrile with sodium and alcohol gives :
rows.solution:
The product is 1-AMINOETHANE, that is ethylamine.

Sodium in alcohol supplies nascent hydrogen, which reduces the nitrile all the way to the primary amine:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na}/\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\)

The carbon count is what settles it. Ethanenitrile has TWO carbons — the methyl and the nitrile carbon — and reduction adds only hydrogens, so the amine must have two carbons as well. 1-Aminopropane has three, so it cannot be the product of a reduction.

The reaction is called MENDIUS REDUCTION, and lithium aluminium hydride or catalytic hydrogenation does the same job.

Ethanoic acid and ethanamide would both require the nitrile to be HYDROLYSED rather than reduced, which needs acid or alkali and water, not a reducing agent.

rows.stem: How many Faradays are required to reduce 1 mol of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ?
rows.solution:
FIVE faradays are required.

One faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons, so the question is really asking how many electrons one mole of permanganate takes up.

Write the half-reaction and balance the charge. Manganese falls from \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) to \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), a change of FIVE units:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

So one mole of permanganate needs five moles of electrons — five faradays, about \(5 \times 96500 = 482500\) coulombs.

This is the number behind every permanganate titration in acidic medium: the reagent is a five-electron oxidising agent, which is why it reacts with iron(II) in a 1 : 5 ratio and with oxalate in a 2 : 5 ratio.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: In a reaction, the initial concentration of the reactants increases four fold and the rate becomes sixteen times its initial value. The order of the reaction is :
rows.solution:
The order is 2.

For a reaction of order \(n\) the rate varies with concentration as
\(\dfrac{\text{Rate}_2}{\text{Rate}_1} = \left(\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_2}{[\mathrm{A}]_1}\right)^{n}\)

Substituting the observation, that a FOURFOLD rise in concentration makes the rate SIXTEEN times larger:
\(16 = 4^{\,n}\)

Since \(16 = 4^2\), the order is \(n = 2\).

The arithmetic can be done by inspection, without logarithms, by asking what power of 4 gives 16. Had the rate risen eightfold, \(8 = 4^{1.5}\) would have given order 1.5; had it merely quadrupled, the order would be 1.

Note that this is the measured order of the reaction as a whole, arrived at by experiment. It cannot be read off a balanced equation, and a fractional value would have been perfectly possible.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives only glucose ?
rows.solution:
MALTOSE gives only glucose on hydrolysis.

Maltose is a DISACCHARIDE built from TWO \(\alpha\)-glucose units, joined \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_4}\), so hydrolysis releases two molecules of the same sugar:
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

The other options fail for two different reasons. SUCROSE gives glucose AND fructose; LACTOSE gives glucose AND galactose — each releases a second sugar besides glucose. GALACTOSE is a MONOSACCHARIDE and cannot be hydrolysed at all.

Starch and cellulose would also have answered the question, both being polymers of glucose alone; maltose is the disaccharide among them, and is in fact the unit from which starch is built.

rows.stem: Deficiency of which of the following vitamins causes Pernicious anaemia ?
rows.solution:
Pernicious anaemia is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN \(\mathrm{B_{12}}\), cyanocobalamin.

It is the only vitamin containing a METAL — cobalt — and it is needed for the maturing of red blood cells. Without it the cells remain large and immature and cannot carry oxygen properly, which is what makes the anaemia "pernicious".

It is found only in foods of ANIMAL origin, so a strict vegetarian diet risks the deficiency; absorption also needs a protein secreted by the stomach, so the disease can arise even with enough in the diet.

Each of the other B vitamins has its own deficiency disease: \(\mathrm{B_1}\) gives beri-beri, \(\mathrm{B_2}\) gives cheilosis and a sore tongue, \(\mathrm{B_6}\) gives convulsions.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{OH^{-}}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH = CH - COCH_3}\)
This reaction is known as :
rows.solution:
This is CROSS-ALDOL CONDENSATION.

An aldol condensation joins two carbonyl compounds through the \(\alpha\) carbon of one and the carbonyl carbon of the other. When the TWO partners are DIFFERENT, the reaction is a CROSS aldol.

Here they are different in a way that makes the outcome clean. Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen — the only carbon beside its carbonyl is part of the ring — so it cannot supply the carbanion and can only act as the ELECTROPHILE. Propanone has \(\alpha\) hydrogens and supplies the carbanion.

So only ONE product is possible, rather than the four a cross aldol between two enolisable partners would give. Loss of water from the initial addition product creates the conjugated double bond shown.

A plain aldol condensation would need the SAME compound as both partners, and the Cannizzaro reaction needs a strong base with an aldehyde having no \(\alpha\) hydrogen and no enolisable partner present.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: In which of the following does the central atom exhibit an oxidation state of +3 ?
rows.solution:
The central atom is \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\).

Work each one out by letting the ligand charges and the overall charge fix the metal's.

Oxalate carries \(-2\), and three of them give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron must be \(+3\). That is the answer.

In \(\mathrm{K_2[Ni(CN)_4]}\) two potassiums outside make the complex ion \(2-\); four cyanides give \(-4\), so nickel is \(+2\).

In \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) four potassiums make the ion \(4-\); six cyanides give \(-6\), so iron here is \(+2\) — the same metal as the answer but a different state, which is the trap.

In \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}\) ammonia is neutral, so copper simply carries the \(+2\).

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When NaCl is added to water, a depression in freezing point is observed.
Reason (R) : The lowering of vapour pressure of a solution causes depression in the freezing point.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Sodium chloride is a non-volatile solute, so adding it to water DOES depress the freezing point — the Assertion holds, and sharply, since each formula unit gives two ions.

The Reason states the mechanism correctly. A liquid freezes at the temperature where the vapour pressure of the LIQUID equals that of the SOLID. Adding a non-volatile solute LOWERS the vapour pressure of the liquid at every temperature, so the two curves now meet at a LOWER temperature — and that new meeting point is the new freezing point.

So the depression is not a separate phenomenon standing beside the lowering of vapour pressure; it is a CONSEQUENCE of it. The same lowering also explains the elevation of boiling point, which is why all four colligative properties are treated together.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) for weak electrolytes shows a sharp decrease when the electrolytic solution is diluted.
Reason (R) : For weak electrolytes, degree of dissociation increases with dilution of solution.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

For a weak electrolyte the molar conductivity shows a sharp INCREASE on dilution, not a decrease — so the Assertion has the direction wrong.

The Reason is correct, and it is exactly why. A weak electrolyte is only partly dissociated, and dilution shifts that equilibrium towards MORE dissociation, so the number of ions furnished by one mole of electrolyte RISES steeply. Since molar conductivity counts the conductance per mole of electrolyte, it rises with them.

The rise is steepest near infinite dilution, which is what makes the curve run almost parallel to the vertical axis there — and why \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for a weak electrolyte cannot be found by extrapolating the graph, but must come from Kohlrausch's law instead.

A STRONG electrolyte behaves differently: it is fully dissociated at all dilutions, so its molar conductivity rises only slightly, and only because the ions stop interfering with one another.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Zr and Hf have almost identical radii.
Reason (R) : Both Zr and Hf exhibit similar properties.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Zirconium and hafnium do have almost identical radii — about 160 pm each — although hafnium lies a whole period below. The cause is the LANTHANOID CONTRACTION: the fourteen lanthanoids intervene between them, and across that series the \(4f\) electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the steady rise in nuclear charge pulls the outer shells in and cancels the increase in size expected from the extra period.

The Reason is also true — the two elements are so alike that they occur together in nature and are notoriously difficult to separate.

But it does not EXPLAIN the Assertion; it has cause and effect the wrong way round. The similar radii are the CAUSE and the similar properties the CONSEQUENCE, not the other way about. Had the Reason named the lanthanoid contraction, it would have been the correct explanation.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Monobromination of aniline can be conveniently done by protecting the amino group by acetylation.
Reason (R) : Acetylation decreases the activating effect of the amino group.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The amino group activates the ring so powerfully that bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline at once, with no way to stop at one substitution. ACETYLATION solves this, and the Reason names why it works.

In acetanilide the nitrogen's lone pair is shared between the ring and the neighbouring CARBONYL group, which competes for it. Less density reaches the ring, so the group is still ortho, para directing but much LESS activating — enough for a single bromination, not for three.

Bromination then goes mainly PARA, the ortho positions being blocked by the bulky acetyl group, and hydrolysis with acid or alkali removes the acetyl to give p-bromoaniline.

The acetyl group is therefore a PROTECTING group: attached before the reaction and removed after, having changed the outcome without appearing in the product.

rows.stem: An alkyl halide (A) of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{13}Cl}\) on treatment with alcoholic KOH gives two isomeric alkenes (B) and (C) of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}\). Both alkenes on hydrogenation give 2,3-dimethylbutane. Write the structures of (A), (B) and (C).
rows.solution:
The hydrogenation product identifies the carbon SKELETON, since hydrogenation changes no bonds between carbons. Both alkenes give 2,3-dimethylbutane, so all three compounds are built on \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}CH(CH_3)_2}\).

The formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{13}Cl}\) is saturated, so (A) is that skeleton with a chlorine on it. For elimination to give TWO different alkenes, the chlorine must sit where two different \(\beta\) carbons are available — at a carbon bearing the methyl group:

(A) is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(Cl){-}CH(CH_3)_2}\), 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.

Removing a hydrogen from the neighbouring \(\mathrm{CH}\) gives the more substituted alkene, which is the major product by Saytzeff's rule:

(B) is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}C(CH_3)_2}\), 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

Removing one from a methyl group instead gives the less substituted alkene:

(C) is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(CH_3){-}CH(CH_3)_2}\), 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

Both add hydrogen to give 2,3-dimethylbutane, as the question requires.

rows.stem: Define Azeotrope. What type of azeotrope is formed by negative deviation from Raoult's law ? Give an example.
rows.solution:
An AZEOTROPE is a binary mixture of liquids that boils at a CONSTANT temperature and distils UNCHANGED — the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so the components cannot be separated by fractional distillation.

That last point is the practical meaning. Ordinary distillation works because the vapour is richer in the more volatile component; at the azeotropic composition it is not, so the distillation makes no further progress.

A NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law gives a MAXIMUM BOILING azeotrope. The unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than the like ones do, so the vapour pressure is lower than predicted and the mixture must be heated FURTHER to boil — above the boiling point of either pure component.

EXAMPLE: nitric acid with water, which boils at 393.5 K at a composition of about 68% acid by mass. That is why commercial nitric acid comes at that strength.

rows.stem:
Name the cell which :
(a) was used in Apollo Space programme.
(b) is used in automobiles and inverters.
(c) is suitable for hearing aids and watches.
(d) does not give a steady potential and is used in transistors.
rows.solution:
(a) FUEL CELL — the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell powered the Apollo space programme, and the water it produced was drunk by the crew. It converts the energy of combustion of a fuel directly into electrical energy, with the reactants fed in continuously.

(b) LEAD STORAGE BATTERY — used in automobiles and inverters. Its virtue is being RECHARGEABLE: the electrode reactions reverse when current is passed the other way, so the cell can be used again and again.

(c) MERCURY CELL — suitable for hearing aids and watches, because it gives a CONSTANT potential throughout its life. The reason is that its overall reaction involves no ion whose concentration changes.

(d) DRY CELL, the Leclanche cell — used in transistors and torches. Its potential FALLS steadily during use, because ammonia produced at the cathode and the rising zinc ion concentration at the anode both shift the electrode potentials as the cell discharges.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate constant for the first order decomposition of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) is given by the following equation :
\(\log \mathrm{k} = 23{\cdot}6 - \frac{2 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}}{\mathrm{T}}\)
Calculate \(\mathrm{E_a}\) for this reaction.
\([\mathrm{R} = 8{\cdot}314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}]\)
rows.solution:
Compare the given equation with the Arrhenius equation in logarithmic form:
\(\log k = \log \mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,\mathrm{R}\,\mathrm{T}}\)

The equation supplied is \(\log k = 23{\cdot}6 - \dfrac{2 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}}{\mathrm{T}}\), so the two terms match up directly:
\(\dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,\mathrm{R}} = 2 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}\)

Therefore
\(E_a = 2{\cdot}303 \times 8{\cdot}314 \times 2 \times 10^4\)

\(E_a = 3{\cdot}830 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is about 383 kJ per mole

The method is worth noting: no rate constants are needed and no temperature is substituted. The activation energy is read straight off the SLOPE of the given relation, since a plot of \(\log k\) against \(1/\mathrm{T}\) is a straight line whose slope is \(-E_a/2{\cdot}303\mathrm{R}\), and the intercept 23.6 is \(\log \mathrm{A}\).

rows.stem:
Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_2 = CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^{+}}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)
rows.solution:
The acid first protonates water, \(\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_3O^+}\), and the hydronium ion is the proton source for what follows.

STEP 1 — protonation of the alkene. The \(\pi\) electrons of the double bond attack a proton, and the carbon left without them becomes a CARBOCATION. This step is SLOW and rate determining:
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_3O^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

STEP 2 — nucleophilic attack by water. A lone pair on the oxygen attacks the positive carbon, giving a PROTONATED ALCOHOL:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

STEP 3 — deprotonation. A second water molecule removes the extra proton, giving the alcohol and regenerating the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_3O^+}\)

The acid appears in step 1 and returns in step 3, so it is a true CATALYST and only a trace is needed. Notice also that this mechanism is the exact REVERSE of the acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol — the same three steps run backwards, which is why the temperature and the amount of water decide which way the reaction goes.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the products of the following reactions :
(i) Benzaldehyde \(\xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{Conc. NaOH}}\)
(ii) Cyclopentanone \(+\ \mathrm{H_2NNH - CO - NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^{+}}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Both reactants are DRAWN, not named: (i) is a benzene ring bearing —CHO and (ii) is a cyclopentane ring bearing =O, each followed by its printed reagent arrow. The stem above names them in words (benzaldehyde, cyclopentanone), which is faithful to what the drawings show, but the printed reaction block should be attached as the crop. Page idx 12, upper half.
rows.solution:
(i) Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN, so it cannot undergo aldol condensation. With concentrated alkali it undergoes CANNIZZARO'S REACTION instead — a disproportionation in which one molecule is oxidised and another reduced:
\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\)

The products are BENZYL ALCOHOL and SODIUM BENZOATE, the free acid being obtained on acidification.

(ii) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water:
\(\mathrm{C_5H_8{=}O} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_5H_8{=}N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is CYCLOPENTANONE SEMICARBAZONE.

Only ONE of semicarbazide's two nitrogen atoms attacks — the terminal \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) of the hydrazine part. The other is attached to the carbonyl group and its lone pair is delocalised, so it is not nucleophilic enough.

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem:
Do the following conversions in not more than two steps :
(i) Toluene to Benzoic acid
(ii) Benzaldehyde to 1-Phenylethanol
rows.solution:
(i) TOLUENE TO BENZOIC ACID, in one step. Alkaline permanganate oxidises the whole side chain to a carboxyl group, and acidification frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

The oxidation attacks the BENZYLIC carbon, and it does so however long the side chain is — ethylbenzene gives the same product.

(ii) BENZALDEHYDE TO 1-PHENYLETHANOL, in two steps. The product is a SECONDARY alcohol with one carbon more than the aldehyde, so a Grignard reagent must add a methyl group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3MgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OH)CH_3}\)

Counting carbons is what chooses the method: eight in the product against seven in the aldehyde means a carbon must be ADDED, so reduction alone would not serve.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination entities :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl(NO_2)]Cl}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Work out the oxidation state first. The five ammine ligands are neutral; the chlorido and nitrito ligands inside give \(-1\) each; the chloride outside gives \(-1\). For the whole compound to be neutral, cobalt must be \(+3\).

Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order, regardless of their charge, and the counter ion is named last:
TETRAAMMINECHLORIDONITRITO-N-COBALT(III) CHLORIDE

The "N" records which atom of the nitrite the cobalt is bonded to, since that ligand is ambidentate. Bound through oxygen it would be the nitrito-O isomer, a different compound of the same formula.

(b) The two chlorido ligands give \(-2\), ethane-1,2-diamine is neutral, and the ion carries \(+2\), so platinum is \(+4\).

The prefix for a complex ligand whose own name contains a multiplying prefix is BIS rather than "di", and the ligand name is enclosed in brackets:
DICHLORIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)PLATINUM(IV) ION

Alphabetical order uses the name of the ligand itself, so "chlorido" is placed before "ethane-1,2-diamine" and the prefixes are ignored in the ordering.

rows.stem:
(i) Write hydroboration-oxidation reaction with an example.
(ii) Write the products of the following reaction :
Anisole \(+\ \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow\)
(iii) Why is p-nitrophenol more acidic than phenol ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (ii)'s reactant is DRAWN as a benzene ring bearing —OCH3; the stem above names it in words (anisole), which is what the drawing shows, but the printed reaction block should be attached as the crop. Page idx 12, lower half.
rows.solution:
(i) HYDROBORATION-OXIDATION adds water across a double bond with ANTI-MARKOVNIKOV orientation, in two stages. Diborane adds first, the electron deficient boron attaching to the LESS substituted carbon; alkaline hydrogen peroxide then replaces the boron by a hydroxyl in the same place:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} (\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O_2}/\mathrm{OH^-}} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)

Propene therefore gives PROPAN-1-OL, where acid-catalysed hydration would have given propan-2-ol.

(ii) Hydrobromic acid cleaves the ether at the METHYL carbon, giving PHENOL and BROMOMETHANE:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3Br}\)

The bond from oxygen to the ring carbon has partial double bond character from resonance and is not broken; a ring carbon is not open to attack in any case.

(iii) Because the NITRO GROUP stabilises the p-nitrophenoxide ion.

Acidity is decided by the stability of the anion. The nitro group withdraws electron density both inductively and by RESONANCE, and from the para position its resonance reaches the phenoxide oxygen directly — the negative charge is delocalised onto the nitro oxygens as well as around the ring.

The charge is therefore spread more widely than in phenoxide itself, the anion is more stable, and the acid is stronger: \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 7.1 against phenol's 10.0.

rows.stem:
(i) What happens when phenol reacts with
(1) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\), and
(2) \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) in presence of aqueous NaOH followed by acidification ?
Write equations only.
(ii) Why does the reaction of \(\mathrm{CH_3ONa}\) with \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - Br}\) give 2-methylpropene and not \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - OCH_3}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Concentrated nitric acid nitrates phenol at all three activated positions, the hydroxyl being strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{HNO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{conc.}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, picric acid.

(2) Chloroform with aqueous sodium hydroxide, followed by acidification, is the REIMER-TIEMANN reaction:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} + 3\mathrm{NaCl} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is salicylaldehyde — 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde — the attacking species being dichlorocarbene generated from the chloroform.

(ii) Because methoxide is a strong BASE and the substrate is TERTIARY, so ELIMINATION beats substitution.

Two effects push the same way. The tertiary carbon is surrounded by three methyl groups, so a nucleophile cannot reach it for backside attack and substitution is sterically blocked. Meanwhile the \(\beta\) hydrogens are fully exposed, and the base removes one readily.

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}Br} + \mathrm{CH_3O^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{Br^-}\)

This is why the Williamson synthesis must be planned with the halide PRIMARY and the alkoxide carrying the bulk — to make that ether one would use tert-butoxide with bromomethane, not the reverse.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(a) Benzyl chloride is highly reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction.
(b) \((\pm)\)-Butan-2-ol is optically inactive, though it contains a chiral carbon atom.
(c) Chloroform is stored in closed dark coloured bottles.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the BENZYL CARBOCATION is stabilised by RESONANCE.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction goes through a carbocation, so its rate depends on how easily that cation forms. When benzyl chloride ionises, the positive charge on the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group is not confined there — it is delocalised into the ring, spreading to the ortho and para carbons:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \longleftrightarrow\) three further structures with the charge on ring carbons

A charge shared over four carbons is far more stable than one on a single primary carbon, so the cation forms easily and the reaction is fast — faster than for an ordinary primary halide, which would barely react by this route at all.

(b) Because it is a RACEMIC MIXTURE — the \(\pm\) sign says so.

Butan-2-ol does contain a chiral carbon, so each individual molecule IS optically active. But the \((\pm)\) form contains the two enantiomers in EQUAL amounts, and they rotate plane polarised light by equal angles in OPPOSITE directions.

The two rotations cancel exactly, so the mixture shows no net rotation. The inactivity is a property of the MIXTURE, not of the molecules in it — which is why it is called EXTERNAL compensation.

(c) Because chloroform is slowly OXIDISED by air and light to PHOSGENE, which is highly poisonous:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

The dark bottle excludes the light that drives the reaction, and the bottles are kept FULL and closed so that little air remains. A small quantity of ethanol is also added, which converts any phosgene formed into harmless ethyl carbonate.

rows.stem:
Answer any three of the following questions :
(a) Explain the type of hybridization in \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) on the basis of valence bond theory. (Given : Atomic number of Fe = 26)
(b) Draw the geometrical isomers of \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}}\) ion.
(c) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) is paramagnetic while \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why ?
(d) Name the type of isomerism when ambidentate ligands are attached to central metal ion. Give one example of ambidentate ligand.
rows.solution:
(a) Iron is atomic number 26, so the atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2\). Six cyanides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — five orbitals, one electron each.

Cyanide is a STRONG FIELD ligand. It forces those five electrons to pair up into the lower three d orbitals, leaving \(t_{2g}^5\) with ONE unpaired electron and TWO inner \(3d\) orbitals empty.

Those two vacant \(3d\) orbitals, together with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\), give \(d^2sp^3\) hybridisation — SIX equivalent orbitals pointing to the corners of an OCTAHEDRON, each accepting a lone pair from a cyanide.

Because INNER d orbitals are used, this is an inner orbital or LOW SPIN complex; it is paramagnetic to the extent of one unpaired electron, \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M.

(b) The ion is octahedral, with two chlorido ligands and two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands spanning adjacent positions. The two chlorides can be arranged in two ways:

CIS — the two chlorido ligands ADJACENT, at \(90^{\circ}\) to each other, with the two chelate rings filling the remaining positions. This form has no plane of symmetry and is itself optically active.

TRANS — the two chlorido ligands OPPOSITE, at \(180^{\circ}\), with the two chelate rings lying in the plane between them. This form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

(c) Because CHLORIDE is a WEAK field ligand and CARBON MONOXIDE is a STRONG one.

In \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is \(+2\), that is \(3d^8\). Chloride splits the d orbitals only weakly and does not force pairing, so TWO electrons remain unpaired and the ion is PARAMAGNETIC, with \(sp^3\) hybridisation.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is ZERO, that is \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the d set, giving \(3d^{10}\) with every electron PAIRED, so the complex is DIAMAGNETIC — again \(sp^3\), and again tetrahedral.

The geometry is the same; the electron count and the field strength are what differ.

(d) LINKAGE ISOMERISM.

It arises when an AMBIDENTATE ligand — one with two different donor atoms — binds through either of them. Example: the NITRITE ion, which binds through nitrogen as nitrito-N or through oxygen as nitrito-O. Thiocyanate and cyanide behave the same way.

rows.stem:
If benzoic acid (M = 122 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) is associated into a dimer when dissolved in benzene and the osmotic pressure of a solution of \(6{\cdot}1\) g of benzoic acid in 100 mL benzene is \(6{\cdot}5\) atm at \(27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), then what is the percentage association of benzoic acid ?
(Given : R = \(0{\cdot}0821\) L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Use the osmotic pressure equation with the van't Hoff factor included:
\(\pi = i\,\dfrac{n_B}{\mathrm{V}}\mathrm{RT} = i\,\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{\mathrm{V\ in\ mL}}\times \mathrm{RT}\)

Substituting the data, with the temperature converted to 300 K:
\(6{\cdot}5 = i \times \dfrac{6{\cdot}1}{122} \times \dfrac{1000}{100} \times 0{\cdot}0821 \times 300\)

The concentration is \(\frac{6.1}{122} \times \frac{1000}{100} = 0{\cdot}5\) mol per litre, so the bracket evaluates to \(0{\cdot}5 \times 0{\cdot}0821 \times 300 = 12{\cdot}315\) atm:
\(i = \dfrac{6{\cdot}5}{12{\cdot}315} = 0{\cdot}528\)

For ASSOCIATION of \(n\) molecules into one, the degree of association follows from
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}}\)

With \(n = 2\) for a dimer:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1 - 0{\cdot}528}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}472}{0{\cdot}5} = 0{\cdot}944\)

PERCENTAGE ASSOCIATION \(= 94{\cdot}4\%\)

The sign is the check: association REDUCES the particle count, so \(i\) must come out below 1 and the observed osmotic pressure must be SMALLER than the formula predicts, as it is here — 6.5 atm against 12.3.

rows.stem:
The following data were obtained during the first order thermal decomposition of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\) at a constant volume :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl\,(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_4\,(g)} + \mathrm{HCl\,(g)}\)

| Experiment | Time (\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\)) | Total pressure (atm) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | \(0{\cdot}4\) |
| 2 | 100 | \(0{\cdot}6\) |

Calculate the rate constant.
(Given : log 2 = \(0{\cdot}3010\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}4771\), log 4 = \(0{\cdot}6021\))
rows.solution:
The reaction turns ONE mole of gas into TWO, so the total pressure RISES as it proceeds, and that rise measures how much has decomposed.

Let \(x\) be the pressure of chloroethane that has decomposed. It is replaced by \(x\) of ethene plus \(x\) of hydrogen chloride, so the total is \(p_i + x\):
\(0{\cdot}6 = 0{\cdot}4 + x\), giving \(x = 0{\cdot}2\) atm

The reactant remaining is therefore \(0{\cdot}4 - 0{\cdot}2 = 0{\cdot}2\) atm. Since pressure is proportional to concentration for an ideal gas at constant volume, the first order equation can be used with pressures directly:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_i - x} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{100}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}4}{0{\cdot}2}\)
\(= \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}3010}{100}\)

\(k = 6{\cdot}93 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

A check without arithmetic: the reactant has fallen to exactly HALF in 100 s, so 100 s IS the half-life, and \(k = 0{\cdot}693/100\) gives the same answer.

The common error is to put the TOTAL pressure 0.6 into the equation. The rate law needs the pressure of the REACTANT alone, which is falling while the total rises.

rows.stem: What is the difference between a glycosidic linkage and peptide linkage ?
rows.context:
Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose.

Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one.
rows.solution:
A PEPTIDE linkage joins two AMINO ACIDS. It is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO{-}NH}-\), formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next and water is lost — so the bridging atom is NITROGEN.

A GLYCOSIDIC linkage joins two MONOSACCHARIDES. It is formed when the hydroxyl groups of two sugar units condense with the loss of water, leaving an OXYGEN atom bridging them.

The two differ in both respects: in WHAT they join — amino acids against sugars — and in the ATOM that does the joining. One builds proteins, the other builds disaccharides and polysaccharides.

rows.stem: Which amino acids are called essential amino acids ?
rows.context:
Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose.

Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one.
rows.solution:
ESSENTIAL amino acids are those the human body CANNOT SYNTHESISE, and which must therefore be obtained from the DIET.

There are ten of them, valine, leucine and lysine among them.

The rest are NON-ESSENTIAL: the body can make them from other compounds, so a shortage in the diet does not matter. Glycine and alanine are examples.

The distinction is about our own metabolism, not about how important the acids are — every one of the twenty is needed to build proteins, and a diet short of any ESSENTIAL one will limit protein synthesis whatever else it contains.

rows.stem: What are the common types of secondary structures of proteins ? Write any two forces which stabilise the secondary and tertiary structures of protein.
rows.context:
Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose.

Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one.
rows.solution:
The common secondary structures are the \(\alpha\)-HELIX and the \(\beta\)-PLEATED SHEET.

In the \(\alpha\)-helix the polypeptide chain coils clockwise, and each \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) hydrogen bonds to the \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) four residues further along the SAME chain. In the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet the chains are stretched side by side, and the hydrogen bonds run BETWEEN neighbouring chains.

FORCES THAT STABILISE the secondary and tertiary structures, any two of:

HYDROGEN BONDS, between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) and \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) groups of the backbone — the force holding both secondary structures in shape.

DISULPHIDE BRIDGES, covalent \(-\mathrm{S{-}S}-\) links formed between two cysteine residues that may lie far apart along the chain.

ELECTROSTATIC ATTRACTION, between oppositely charged side chains, and VAN DER WAALS FORCES between the non-polar ones.

rows.stem: Define denaturation of protein with an example. During denaturation which structures of protein lose their biological activity ?
rows.context:
Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose.

Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one.
rows.solution:
DENATURATION is the loss of a protein's NATIVE three-dimensional shape, and with it its BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY, when the protein is subjected to a change of temperature or of pH.

EXAMPLE: the CURDLING OF MILK when it turns sour, the acid produced by bacteria denaturing the milk protein. Boiling an egg is the same process — the clear white coagulates into an opaque solid, and it does not become clear again on cooling.

The SECONDARY and TERTIARY structures are the ones destroyed. The hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges and electrostatic attractions that held the folded shape are broken, and the chain uncoils into a random shape.

The PRIMARY structure SURVIVES, because the peptide bonds that hold the sequence together are covalent and far stronger. Nothing is lost from the chain; only its folding is — and that is enough, because a protein's activity depends on its shape.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values in aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\)
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, imides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and hydrogen bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Presence of amino group in aromatic ring enhances reactivity of the aromatic amines. Aryl diazonium salts provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes by reductive removal of the diazo group.
rows.solution:
Increasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\):
\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)

Read the direction first. A LOWER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a STRONGER base, so increasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means DECREASING basicity, and the answer runs from the strongest base to the weakest.

In AQUEOUS solution two opposing effects decide the order, and neither wins outright.

Each ethyl group RELEASES electron density to the nitrogen, making the lone pair more available — this favours the tertiary amine.

But the conjugate acid must be STABILISED BY HYDROGEN BONDING to water, and that needs hydrogens on the nitrogen. The primary amine's cation has three, the secondary's two, the tertiary's only one — this favours the primary amine. The three bulky ethyl groups also obstruct the approach of a proton.

The SECONDARY amine, having a reasonable share of both advantages, is the strongest base; the tertiary comes next; the primary is the weakest. In the GAS PHASE, where no solvent can hydrogen bond, the order is purely inductive and the tertiary amine is strongest.

rows.stem: Aniline on nitration gives a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline, though amino group is o/p directing. Why ?
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, imides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and hydrogen bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Presence of amino group in aromatic ring enhances reactivity of the aromatic amines. Aryl diazonium salts provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes by reductive removal of the diazo group.
rows.solution:
Because nitration is carried out in a STRONGLY ACIDIC medium, in which aniline exists largely as the ANILINIUM ION.

Nitric acid with sulphuric acid protonates the amino group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3}\)

That changes the directing behaviour completely. A free \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group DONATES its lone pair to the ring and is ortho, para directing. In \(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{N}}\mathrm{H_3}\) the lone pair is gone and the group carries a positive charge, so it WITHDRAWS density powerfully and becomes META directing, like the nitro group itself.

So the reaction mixture contains two species reacting in parallel: the small amount of free aniline giving ortho and para products, and the protonated form giving the meta product. The result is a mixture — roughly 47% of it meta, a proportion far higher than a simple ortho, para director would give.

This is also why ACETYLATION is used when a clean para product is wanted: acetanilide is not basic enough to be protonated, so the directing effect survives the acidic conditions.

rows.stem: An aromatic compound 'A' of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\) on treatment with aqueous ammonia and heating forms compound 'B'. Compound 'B' on heating with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) and aqueous KOH gives a compound 'C' of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\). Write the structures of A, B and C.
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, imides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and hydrogen bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Presence of amino group in aromatic ring enhances reactivity of the aromatic amines. Aryl diazonium salts provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes by reductive removal of the diazo group.
rows.solution:
The molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\) with an aromatic ring and two oxygens points to BENZOIC ACID.

Aqueous ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating to give the AMIDE:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), benzoic acid
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide

Bromine with aqueous potassium hydroxide is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, which converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

The carbon count is what confirms the last step: the formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\) has six carbons where the amide had seven, and losing exactly one carbon is the signature of this reaction.

Presence of amino group in aromatic ring enhances reactivity of the aromatic amines. Aryl diazonium salts provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes by reductive removal of the diazo group.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Both reactants are DRAWN, not named: (1) is a benzene ring bearing —NH2 and (2) is a benzene ring bearing —N2(+) Cl(-), each followed by its printed reagent arrow. The stem above names them in words (aniline, benzenediazonium chloride), which is what the drawings show, but the printed reaction block should be attached as the crop. Page idx 18, lower half.
rows.solution:
(1) Bromine in AQUEOUS solution brominates aniline at all three activated positions at once, the amino group being so strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3NH_2} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

The product is 2,4,6-TRIBROMOANILINE, which separates as a white precipitate. Stopping at one bromine requires the amino group to be acetylated first.

(2) Fluoroboric acid precipitates the diazonium salt as its FLUOROBORATE, and heating that with sodium nitrite and copper replaces the diazonium group by a nitro group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HBF_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+BF_4^-} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{Cu}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{NaBF_4}\)

The product is NITROBENZENE. Note that heating the fluoroborate ALONE, without the nitrite, gives fluorobenzene instead — the Balz-Schiemann reaction, which is the usual way of putting fluorine onto a ring.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Al\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Al}^{3+}\,(0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Ni\,(s)}\)
[Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Al}^{3+}/\mathrm{Al}} = -\,1{\cdot}66\) V, \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V, log 10 = 1]
(ii) With the help of a graph explain why it is not possible to determine \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\) for a weak electrolyte by extrapolating the molar conductivity \((\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}})\) versus \(\mathrm{C}^{1/2}\) curve as for strong electrolyte.
rows.solution:
(i) Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is on the left, so aluminium is oxidised and nickel reduced.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = -0{\cdot}25 - (-1{\cdot}66) = 1{\cdot}41\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing the electrons gives the cell reaction \(2\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{Ni^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Ni}\), so \(n = 6\). Solids do not appear in the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Al^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}41 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log\dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{(10^{-1})^3} = 1{\cdot}41 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{6}\log 10^{-3}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}41 + \dfrac{0{\cdot}059 \times 3}{6} = 1{\cdot}41 + 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 1{\cdot}4395\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note the EXPONENTS: each concentration is raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation, so the quotient is \(10^{-6}/10^{-3}\), not \(10^{-3}/10^{-1}\).

(ii) Because a weak electrolyte's curve NEVER MEETS the vertical axis — it rises without limit as the concentration approaches zero.

For a STRONG electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) plotted against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is a straight line over a good range, because full dissociation means the only thing changing is how much the ions interfere with one another. Extrapolating that line back to \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}} = 0\) gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly.

For a WEAK electrolyte the curve is quite different. Its molar conductivity changes because the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION changes, and near infinite dilution that degree rises so steeply that the curve becomes almost PARALLEL to the vertical axis. There is no straight portion to extrapolate and no intercept to read.

So \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for a weak electrolyte must be found INDIRECTLY, from KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW — by adding the limiting molar conductivities of its ions, each obtained from strong electrolytes that do give a straight line.

rows.stem:
(i) The molar conductivities of \(\mathrm{NH_4^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ion are \(73{\cdot}8\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(76{\cdot}2\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. The conductivity of \(0{\cdot}1\) M \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) is \(1{\cdot}29 \times 10^{-2}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation.
(ii) Calculate the half-cell potential at 298 K for the reaction
\(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}\)
if \([\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}] = 0{\cdot}1\) M and \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\) V.
rows.solution:
(i) First find the limiting molar conductivity by Kohlrausch's law, adding the two ionic contributions:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 73{\cdot}8 + 76{\cdot}2 = 150{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Then the observed molar conductivity from the measured conductivity. The factor of 1000 converts litres to cubic centimetres, since \(\kappa\) is per centimetre while the concentration is per litre:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}29 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}1}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 129\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{129}{150} = 0{\cdot}86\)

That is 86% dissociated. The value must come out between 0 and 1, which is the check — a ratio above 1 would mean the measurement or the arithmetic was wrong.

(ii) This is a HALF-CELL, so \(n = 2\) and the quotient contains only the zinc ion, solid zinc being omitted:
\(E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}\)
\(= -0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}1} = -0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 1\)

\(E = -0{\cdot}7895\ \mathrm{V}\)

The direction of the shift is worth checking against Le Chatelier's principle. The reaction written consumes zinc ions, so reducing their concentration makes the reduction LESS favourable — and the potential does indeed become more negative than the standard value.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(1) \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) salts are colourless while \(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\) salts are coloured.
(2) \(\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}\) is a strong reducing agent.
(3) Transition metals and their compounds show catalytic activities.
(ii) Write the ionic equations for the oxidizing action of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) in acidic medium with
(1) \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) ion, and
(2) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) ion.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — COMPLETELY FILLED — while \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), partly filled.

Colour in a transition metal salt comes from a D-D TRANSITION: a ligand field splits the five d orbitals into two sets, and an electron absorbs visible light to jump from the lower set to the upper. The colour seen is what remains of the white light after that absorption.

The jump needs an ELECTRON in the lower set and a VACANCY in the upper. The nickel ion has both, so its salts are green. The zinc ion has no vacancy anywhere — every orbital is full — so no such transition is possible and its salts are white.

(2) Because \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is \(3d^4\), and losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\).

In an octahedral aqueous environment that \(3d^3\) arrangement puts one electron in each of the three lower orbitals — a HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}\) set, which is an unusually stable configuration.

Chromium(II) therefore gives up that electron readily, which is what a reducing agent does. Its \(E^{\circ}\) is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V, negative enough that chromium(II) reduces even water, liberating hydrogen.

(3) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds with the reactants.

A catalyst works by offering a path of lower activation energy. A transition metal can do this because it can change oxidation state easily — accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another, returning to its original state at the end. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process works exactly this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are adsorbed and held close together, with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

(ii)(1) Permanganate oxidises iodide to iodine in acidic medium, taking five electrons itself:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} + 10\mathrm{I^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{I_2}\)

(2) With iron(II), each ion gives up one electron:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\)

The 1 : 5 ratio in the second equation is the basis of every permanganate titration of an iron(II) solution.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(i) Name two oxometal anions of the 3d series of the transition metals in which the metal exhibits the oxidation state equal to its group number.
(ii) What is the effect of increasing pH on a solution of \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) ?
(iii) Why is \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) not stable in aqueous solution ?
(iv) Name a member of Lanthanoid series which is well-known to exhibit +4 oxidation state.
(v) Name two elements of 3d series which show anomalous electronic configuration.
rows.solution:
(i) The CHROMATE ion, \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\), in which chromium is \(+6\) — its group number.
The PERMANGANATE ion, \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\), in which manganese is \(+7\) — its group number.

Both reach the maximum state available to them, using every \(4s\) electron and every unpaired \(3d\) electron for bonding. The high state survives only in combination with OXYGEN, which is small and strongly electronegative; no simple halide of manganese(VII) exists.

(ii) The solution turns from ORANGE to YELLOW, dichromate being converted to CHROMATE:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout, so this is not a redox change but an equilibrium that pH controls. Adding acid reverses it and the orange returns.

(iii) Because \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) DISPROPORTIONATES in water:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The driving force is HYDRATION ENERGY. The \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion is smaller and doubly charged, so it is hydrated far more strongly than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) — enough to more than pay for the second ionisation. In the SOLID state, with no water to hydrate anything, copper(I) compounds are perfectly stable.

(iv) CERIUM, which forms \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) and is used as ceric ammonium sulphate, a standard oxidising agent.

(v) CHROMIUM and COPPER. Chromium is \(3d^5 4s^1\) rather than the expected \(3d^4 4s^2\), and copper is \(3d^{10} 4s^1\) rather than \(3d^9 4s^2\) — in each case an electron moves from the \(4s\) orbital to give the extra stability of a HALF-FILLED or COMPLETELY FILLED d subshell.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) Draw structure of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone of benzaldehyde.
(b) Which acid of the following pair is a stronger acid ?
(c) Write the chemical equation involved in Rosenmund's reduction.
(d) Why are \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms of aldehydes and ketones acidic in nature ?
(e) Write a chemical test to distinguish between Benzaldehyde and Benzoic acid.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED for sub-part (b), which is unanswerable from its text alone: the pair is printed ONLY as two drawn para-disubstituted benzene rings joined by the word 'or' — the left ring bears —CF3 and —COOH, the right bears —CH3 and —COOH — and the stem names neither compound. Page idx 22, immediately under sub-part (b).
rows.solution:
(a) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water. The product has the carbonyl oxygen replaced by \(=\mathrm{N{-}NH{-}Ar}\):
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)

The right-hand ring carries its two nitro groups at positions 2 and 4, counting from the carbon bearing the nitrogen. Such derivatives are orange or red crystalline solids with sharp melting points, which is why they were used to identify carbonyl compounds.

(b) The TRIFLUOROMETHYL compound is the stronger acid — 4-(trifluoromethyl)benzoic acid, rather than 4-methylbenzoic acid.

Acid strength is decided by how stable the anion left behind is. Three FLUORINE atoms, each strongly electronegative, withdraw electron density powerfully through the \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect, so the negative charge of the carboxylate is spread away from the oxygens and the anion is stabilised.

A METHYL group does the opposite. It RELEASES electron density by the \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect, intensifying the charge on the carboxylate and destabilising it, so 4-methylbenzoic acid is weaker even than benzoic acid itself.

(c) ROSENMUND'S REDUCTION converts an acyl chloride to an ALDEHYDE by hydrogenation over palladium supported on barium sulphate:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow[\text{barium sulphate}]{\mathrm{Pd}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The catalyst is deliberately POISONED — with sulphur or quinoline, and by the inert barium sulphate support — so that it is not active enough to reduce the aldehyde further to the alcohol. Controlling the catalyst is the whole point of the method.

(d) Because the CARBANION left behind is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

Removing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen leaves a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl, and that charge is immediately delocalised onto the OXYGEN, which is far better able to carry it:
\(\mathrm{{}^-CH_2{-}CH{=}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}O^-}\)

The resulting ENOLATE is stable enough that a base can remove the hydrogen, which it could never do from an ordinary alkane. This acidity is what makes the aldol condensation and \(\alpha\)-halogenation possible.

(e) Use TOLLENS' REAGENT, an ammoniacal solution of silver nitrate. Warmed with BENZALDEHYDE it gives a bright SILVER MIRROR on the inside of the tube, the aldehyde being oxidised to benzoic acid while the silver ion is reduced to the metal. BENZOIC ACID gives no reaction, being already at the acid's oxidation level.

SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE serves equally well and in the opposite direction. Benzoic acid gives brisk EFFERVESCENCE of carbon dioxide, being acidic enough to displace it from the salt; benzaldehyde gives none.
